newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Banks and baked beans make for superstore success.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Banks and baked beans make for superstore success.

text.p: Britain's supermarkets, faced with tight competition in groceries, are stepping further into other retail sectors, with banking and financial services just the latest area on their shopping list.

Beside the baked beans and bananas, shoppers can now also find books, newspapers, videos, over-the-counter medicines and clothes, and the leading supermarkets are also offering services such as banking, insurance and even dry cleaning.

"It's immensely difficult for (supermarkets) to steal customers from one another...(so) they are trying to sell more goods and services to existing customers," said Clive Vaughan of research group Verdict.

None of the four major British supermarkets -- Tesco, J. Sainsbury, ASDA and Safeway -- would give figures for non-food sales but analysts suggested that for ASDA these might account for around 17 percent of its current total.
SUPERMARKETS BRANCH OUT INTO ENTERTAINMENT, BOOK SALES

In the music and entertainment sector, covering compact discs (CDs) through to videos, supermarkets could hold 20 percent of the market by 2000, up from current levels of 15 percent, according to Corporate Intelligence's "UK Retail Report".
The superstores focus generally on sales of Top 40 chart CDs and videos which they can discount because of their capacity to buy in bulk, appealing to the impulse buyer, analysts said.
ASDA, which sells on low price in hypermarket formats, is now the fifth largest player in the British entertainment market, Corporate Intelligence said.
Book sales are another area where supermarkets are taking an ever larger slice of the market following the demise of the Net Book Agreement (NBA), which allowed publishers to set prices.
ASDA, which was a leading force in smashing the NBA, sold seven million books in 1996, up 40 percent on the year earlier, and has increased its range of titles.
"We believe we can grow our books business substantially and grab some serious market share," ASDA's books manager Julian Graham-Rack said in April.

Corporate Intelligence says supermarkets currently have around six percent of the British book market and could increase that to about 10 percent, but add that there is not much chance of taking more because the ranges stocked are limited to best-selling paperbacks and children's books.
INROADS INTO CLOTHING AND PETROL

Clothing is another area where supermarkets have been trying to make inroads and boost sales, with the focus on own-brand basic and children's wear, such as the George range at ASDA and Items at Tesco.
ASDA's chief executive Allan Leighton has said he would like to boost clothing sales to around 10 percent of total, or some 600 million pounds ($980 million) a year.
"Supermarkets' clothing departments benefit greatly from the vast number of shoppers passing through the stores each week," said Corporate Intelligence in a report.

The encroachment of supermarkets into petrol retailing triggered a fierce price war with the oil majors over a year ago, but currently the market appears calmer and supermarkets are now teaming up with petrol retailers to offer convenience shopping on the forecourt.
Supermarkets now hold around 25 percent of the British petrol retailing market.
NEW FORAYS INTO BANKING AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
But the latest and perhaps most publicised moves by the supermarkets have been into banking and financial services.
Sainsbury has launched mortgages to add to credit cards, accounts and insurance, while Tesco has brought out its credit card and said further products would come later.
Sainsbury has set up a joint venture Sainsbury's Bank with Bank of Scotland while Tesco has teamed up with Royal Bank of Scotland and Safeway works with Abbey National.
"Essentially, supermarkets are becoming brand houses," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
"Customers trust the brand to offer service, value for money, and they will translate that into any number of products beyond groceries," he added.

Real food markets are growing by no more than two percent a year, the analyst estimated, making non-food sectors, where margins can be higher than groceries, very attractive in order to boost revenues.
VARIETY STORES LOSE OUT
But there are casualties in this battle of the purse.
"Supermarkets are moving into so many different areas that they are impacting on a wide range of retailers," said Verdict's Vaughan.
Analysts said most at risk were variety stores, such as W.H. Smith and Kingfisher's Woolworth, which carry a range of goods but do not specialise in any particular sector.
David Mackay, managing director of John Menzies Plc, another variety store, admitted in July that "there is increasing competition from the major grocers in almost all commodities".
Corporate Intelligence's report on music retailing put it succinctly when describing the attack from supermarkets in sales of CDs.
"Variety stores are most at risk from the supermarkets, because, in many cases...their product ranges are not sufficiently large to attract real music enthusiasts," the report said.

"A large slice of sales come from shoppers who buy CDs on impulse and they are as likely to do the same in Tesco or ASDA -- perhaps more so because of the frequency with which they visit the supermarkets," it added.
In clothing, chains most at risk include Storehouse chain Bhs and Littlewoods, analysts said, with market leader Marks & Spencer largely unscathed.
Specialist fashion outlets are not being challenged as the supermarkets focus on everyday lines.
But supermarkets are likely to punish retailers who fall behind in product offer and customer service, analysts said.
"If there is weak market share to be taken, they will take it," said the analyst.
"You can effectively fit a Woolworth into a Tesco," he added. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
